newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan poised to unveil 'Big Bang' blueprint.
newsitem.headline: Japan poised to unveil 'Big Bang' blueprint.

text.p: Japan will unveil a blueprint for its much-touted "Big Bang" financial reforms on Friday, but some experts wonder if the nation's financial firms have the right stuff to become world-class competitors any time soon.

Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto has staked much of his still-shaky reputation as a reformer on the deregulation plan, which aims to break down the walls among banks, brokers and insurers, introduce more competition and lure back to Tokyo the business which has left in recent years for greener pastures.

Hashimoto caught sceptics off-guard last November when he first announced a five-year "Big Bang" agenda to make markets "free, fair and global" shortly after a general election ensured him a second term as prime minister.
On Friday, three advisory panels will air recommendations for a laundry-list of reforms now expected to take place mostly by the end of March 2000, two years earlier than first planned.

Among the recommendations Japanese media and financial sources said will be featured are a two-phase liberalisation of stock brokerage commissions, to be completed by the end of 1999; the lifting of a ban on financial holding companies in 1998/99; complete removal of limits on the range of business activities by securities firms' trust bank subsidiaries and banks' securities units in 1999/2000; and permission for non-insurers to enter the insurance sector by the year 2001.

A high-profile scandal at top brokerage Nomura Securities and Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank, meanwhile, has prompted the advisory panel in charge of banking to urge stiffer penalties for breaking the Banking Law, Jiji news agency said on Thursday.

The advisers will also urge letting commercial banks issue straight bonds in 1999/2000 and the introduction in parliament's next regular session of a bill to permit non-bank financial institutions to issue corporate bonds and commercial paper, Jiji said.

To kick off the "Big Bang," parliament last month passed a drastic reform of the Foreign Exchange and Foreign Trade Control Law, to take effect on April 1, 1998, which will remove many outdated regulations on cross-border deals and let firms and individuals deal directly with overseas banks and brokers.

Behind the prescription for sweeping change lies the need to lure back to Tokyo business that has fled to escape high costs and excessive regulation, as well as a desire to force Japan's financial sector to boost its global competitiveness.
The reforms, however, are certain to produce a shake-out in the industry and a lot of pain for unsuccessful players.
"The 'Big Bang'...will see many losers and a small number of winners," said Hiroshi Yamamura, director of the Nippon Life Insurance Research Institute.
Some experts, in fact, doubt whether Japan's long-protected financial institutions can quickly adopt the new mind-set needed to help them hone their competitive edge fast.

Ultimately, success depends on "competitive advantage in terms of technology, or cost of capital, or in terms of superiority of management," said Alicia Ogawa, financial analyst at Salomon Brothers Asia. "It's my belief that none of these things exist in Japan yet...because everything has been kept the same for so long."

"I do not agree with the view that Japanese financial institutions will become internationally competitive in the short-run or the medium-run. If it happens at all, it will take at least a decade," Ogawa added.
Others agree that Japanese financial institutions, many still weighed down by heavy non-performing loans, need to make big changes in how they operate.

"Japanese banks are not accustomed to competing...in terms of product quality so they tend to go for price discounts," said Yoshiyuki Mitsugi, associate director at Standard & Poor's in Tokyo. "I think that is a thing that they have to change."
Government regulators, meanwhile, long trained to protect those they watch over rather than enforce transparent rules with an even hand, also have some serious adapting to do.

"Until now, the regulators' role was one of guiding. The new role will be to check and make sure that the private sector actors keep within the boundaries of the law," said Jesper Koll, chief economist at JP Morgan in Tokyo.
